summary: The article examines how advanced robotics and AI are displacing manufacturing workers, using a BLS report and testimonies from Trenton residents who lost jobs when a factory closed. It covers community responses such as a town hall and grassroots retraining advocacy, stalled legislative talk in Washington, and the debate over whether technology should complement or replace human labor. It argues that an inclusive, collective response is needed so the human element stays central to industry.
one_line: Automation is cutting manufacturing jobs, as seen in Trenton, prompting worker protests, retraining pushes, and debate over technology's role.
key_facts: A Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) report issued October 15th, 2023 said manufacturing human jobs decreased by 5.6% over the past year.
The same BLS report noted investments in automation and robotics rose by 25%.
Michael "Mickey" Davis, 58, is a former line worker at Trenton's biggest auto parts factory, which closed its gates last November due to automation.
Mickey Davis worked 30 years at the factory and said of robots, "they don't complain, don't need breaks... they don't even need the lights on to work!"
Jessica Alverez, a single mother of two and former quality control inspector, said, "It's not just about losing jobs... It's about losing a community."
A town hall meeting was held in Trenton on December 3rd, 2023, where residents voiced concerns to local officials and union representatives.
Ex-machinist Harry Gomez asked at the town hall, "What am I supposed to do now; retrain as a robot?"
By November 2023 new robotic systems could perform complex tasks, making even skilled positions vulnerable.
In January 2024 Washington had murmurs of retraining programs and a 'robot tax', but tangible solutions were sluggish.
Maria Delgado, a former factory worker turned activist, leads grassroots efforts for retraining in fields resistant to automation, saying "We don't want handouts; we just want a fighting chance."
Tech entrepreneur Alex Greene argues technology should be "a tool to enhance human jobs, not replace them," but offers few specifics on striking that balance.
Tech-sector jobs created do not necessarily match the number of manufacturing positions displaced by automation.
